lesson.subject: literacy
lesson.title: Fair or Sneaky?
lesson.subtitle: Term 4 Week 2, Session 4
lesson.footer: Persuasive Writing | Year 5/6 Literacy | Week 2 Session 4

plan.curriculum: English 2.0, Level 5: VC2E5LY09 evaluating information and ideas; VC2E5LA02 moving beyond bare assertions; VC2E5LY08 features used to persuade an audience
plan.shape: spot, name, fix, then play: students catch four sneaky tricks, fix them, then write a sneaky ad and its fair twin, because seeing the trick from the inside is what makes it stick
plan.criticalFeature: strong is not the same as true: a fair argument can be checked
decisionPoints: the choice check: fair and strong
the exit board: a new sneaky claim named and fixed
plan.anchor: Claim it. Prove it. Sell it. Today: sell it fairly, or the reader stops trusting you.
plan.catchUp: Missed earlier sessions? Say: proof must be true and from someone who would know. Today's tricks need nothing from last week.

routineIcons: Write it, chin it, show me
Point to A, B or C
boardSetup: Four trick names on the board: Exaggerating, Everyone's doing it, Name-calling, Mystery source

slides.notes: Open the session. One line: today we become persuasion detectives and catch the sneaky tricks.
Print the Worksheet for everyone, the Extension for early finishers and the Supported Worksheet for those who need it. Write the four trick names on the board.

slides.learningIntention: We are learning to spot sneaky persuasion and make our arguments fair and strong.
successCriteria: I can tell when a claim feels unfair.
I can name a sneaky trick and fix it so it is fair and strong.
I can check my own writing for sneaky tricks.

beats: POINT to the learning intention.
SAY: A good persuader wins without tricks. Today we learn the difference.
SAY: Read the I can lines with me. Everyone, together, on three.
SAY: Noticing a claim feels unfair is where we start.
Naming and fixing the trick is today's main goal.
notes.prep: SC1 noticing unfairness is reachable for all; SC2 name and fix is the core and the exit evidence; SC3 checking their own writing is the stretch.

slides.title: Would you buy it?
lines: 9 out of 10 kids say Zappo cereal makes you smarter!
Everyone's eating it. Don't be left behind!

notes.answer: no - which 10 kids? smarter how? everyone isn't eating it
beats: SAY: A new cereal ad just landed.
Read it like you're about to spend your pocket money.
ASK: Do you believe it?
5 sec. Cue: Thumbs only, voices off. Show me... now.
EXPECT: mostly thumbs down or sideways
ASK: What questions would you ask Zappo?
20 sec. Turn and tell, partner A first.
EXPECT: which kids? who asked them? how do you measure smarter?
SAY: That ad is strong, but it isn't fair. Today we catch the tricks.
trap: believing it because it has a number.
Fix: ask who were the 10 kids? Student sees the number proves nothing.
notes.prep: Low-coupling launch: everyone can doubt an ad. Bridges from Session 3's trustworthy sources. 3 minutes.

slides.meaning: To make something sound bigger or worse than it really is.
slides.example: I've told you a million times! (It was really three.)

notes.answer: to make something sound bigger or worse than it really is
beats: POINT to the word. SAY: Exaggerate. Say it with me. Exaggerate.
SAY: To exaggerate is to make it sound bigger than it really is.
A million times? Probably three.
ASK: Give your partner an exaggeration you've heard at home.
10 sec. Turn and tell, partner B first.
EXPECT: I'm starving; it took forever; everyone has one
trap: thinking exaggeration is the same as lying on purpose.
Fix: say it starts from something true, then stretches it.
notes.prep: The most common sneaky trick, with a home example everyone has heard.

slides.title: Four sneaky tricks
lines: Ask: Is it really everyone? Who said so?
Fair: Many animal experts question whether zoos suit polar bears.

notes.answer: name the trick, ask the checking question, rewrite so it can be checked
beats: POINT to the table.
SAY: Four tricks. Each one has words that give it away.
POINT to Sneaky.
SAY: Everyone hates zoos. Everyone? That's exaggerating.
POINT to Ask, then Fair.
SAY: I ask is it really everyone? No. So I say what's true:
many animal experts question it. Still strong. Now it's fair.
ASK: Which trick uses only lazy people?
5 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: name-calling
trap: fixing a trick by making it weak: Some people maybe don't like zoos.
Fix: keep high modality, swap the untrue word for a true one.
notes.stretch: Explain why a sneaky argument can backfire on the writer.
notes.help: Look for the give-away words in the table first.
notes.prep: The model. Critical feature: strong is not the same as true; a fair argument can be checked.

slides.title: Name the trick
slides.pivot: find the give-away word, then match it in the table
slides.followUp: cold call one board: what's the checking question?

items.text: Every single person in Australia wants plastic banned.
All the high school kids already recycle, so you should too.
Anyone who eats takeaway is lazy and doesn't care about the planet.
Studies prove recycling will fix climate change.
items.say: Two tricks! Which studies? And fix is too big. Tick or fix.

items.text: Drink Zappo water: the only bottle that saves the reef!

say: Five claims. Write the name of the trick.
Use the four names on the board.
trap: writing it's wrong without naming the trick.
Fix: student points to the give-away word, then names it.
notes.stretch: Write the checking question for each.
notes.help: Underline the give-away word before naming.
notes.prep: Guided naming. Item 4 uses two tricks at once. SC2.

slides.title: Which one is fair AND strong?

options.text: Only total idiots still use plastic straws.
options.misconception: name-calling; it insults instead of persuading

options.text: Plastic straws can last for hundreds of years in the ocean.
Everybody knows that straws are the worst thing ever.
options.misconception: exaggerating; everybody and worst can't be checked

notes.answer: B - it can be checked, and it still makes you care
beats: SAY: All three want you to give up straws. Only one plays fair.
ASK: Which one is fair AND strong?
10 sec. Cue: voices off, everyone points to A, B or C.
EXPECT: pointing to B
SCAN the room, back row first.
80%+ -> reveal, cold call: which trick is C?
Less -> ask the checking question for each, re-ask.
REVEAL after pointing is scanned.
SAY: B. You could check it, and hundreds of years still makes us care.
trap: pointing to C because it sounds most certain.
Fix: ask can we check everybody knows? Student re-chooses.
notes.prep: Decision point before the fix round. Under 80% means the first fix is done together on the board.

slides.title: Fix it: fair and strong
slides.pivot: cross out the trick word, swap in something checkable
slides.followUp: cold call two boards: is it still strong?

items.text: All kids are totally addicted to screens.
items.answer: Many kids find it hard to switch off screens.
items.expect: many or some kids + a checkable claim

items.text: Only lazy families drive to school.
items.answer: Walking to school, when it's safe, keeps kids active and cuts pollution.

items.text: Experts say our canteen food is the worst in Victoria.
items.answer: Most of our canteen menu is fried food, and the healthy options sell out first.
items.expect: a checkable fact about our canteen

say: Now fix them. Keep it strong, make it fair.
Write the fair version on your board.
trap: removing the trick and the power: Some kids use screens.
Fix: student adds why it matters, keeps a strong verb.
notes.stretch: Make the fair version more persuasive than the sneaky one.
notes.help: Swap one word: all to many, lazy to a reason.

slides.title: Sneaky ad, fair ad
slides.task: Work through your Worksheet. Finish by writing a sneaky ad with three tricks, then its fair twin.

notes.answer: a sneaky ad with three labelled tricks, and a fair version of the same ad
beats: POINT to the task.
SAY: Have fun with the sneaky one. Rocket socks, self-cleaning lunchboxes, anything.
Then make it honest.
SAY: Read the task, complete each part, check your work.
Finished? Extension next. Everyone, together, on three.
CIRCULATE. Ask: which trick is that? What's the fair version?
ASK: Which version would really sell your product?
5 sec. Cue: Thumbs only, voices off. Thumbs up for fair... now.
EXPECT: most thumbs up
TIME 15 minutes. At 12, two students read both versions aloud.
trap: Fix: student keeps one strong verb and one feeling word in the fair ad.
notes.stretch: Extension: question ad claims, then write a fair ad that wins.
notes.help: Supported Worksheet: fair-or-sneaky choices, a first fix done, a frame.
notes.prep: Independent creative application. Writing the tricks from the inside cements them. SC2 and SC3.

slides.extendedTask: a worksheet ending in a sneaky ad with labelled tricks and its fair twin

slides.title: Show what you know
questions: All dog owners are selfish because some dogs bark at night.
Name the trick. Then rewrite it so it is fair and strong.

notes.answer: exaggerating and name-calling. e.g. Barking at night can keep neighbours awake
beats: SAY: A brand new sneaky claim. Catch it and fix it.
ASK: Name the trick, then write the fair version.
60 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: name-calling or exaggerating, plus a checkable rewrite
RECORD who names it but can't fix it. Monday's small group.
trap: naming the trick, then keeping all and selfish.
Fix: none now, record the name.
notes.prep: Exit evidence for SC2 on a new claim. One board per student.

slides.reflectionPrompt: Where have you seen a sneaky trick outside school this week? Tell your partner.

notes.answer: open - ads, games, social media, packaging
beats: SAY: Let's read our I can lines together. Everyone, together, on three.
ASK: How sure are you that you can name and fix a sneaky trick?
5 sec. Cue: Thumbs only, voices off. Show me... now.
EXPECT: thumbs up, sideways or down
RECORD each thumb down beside the exit boards.
ASK: Where have you seen a sneaky trick outside school?
20 sec. Turn and tell, partner A first.
EXPECT: a game ad said everyone is playing it
notes.prep: Self-assessment read beside the exit boards. Week 2 ends with a mentor text, upgraded words, a proof paragraph and a fair-ad check in every book. SC2.

resources.label: Worksheet
resources.description: Your turn: name the trick, choose the fair one, fix sneaky claims, then write a sneaky ad and its fair twin.
resources.title: Fair or Sneaky?
resources.subtitle: Strong is not the same as true.

items.prompt: Name the trick: exaggerating, everyone's doing it, name-calling or mystery source.
rows: Only greedy people drive big cars.
Experts say our pool is unsafe.
All the cool kids have a smartwatch.
This is the best park in the universe.
Studies show cats are smarter than dogs.
answers: Only greedy people drive big cars.
Experts say our pool is unsafe.
All the cool kids have a smartwatch.
This is the best park in the universe.
Studies show cats are smarter than dogs.

example.prompt: Which is fair? A: Everyone loves pools. B: Our town pool gets 500 visits a week.

options: Only lazy kids get driven to school.
Walking to school, when it's safe, keeps kids fit.
Every single car trip ruins the planet!
items.explain: It can be checked and it gives a reason, with no insult.

items.prompt: Max's ad uses a sneaky trick. Find it and fix it.
work: Every kid in Australia is buying Rocket Socks!
items.answer: Exaggerating. Fix: Rocket Socks are soft, warm and come in 12 colours.

example.prompt: Sneaky: Nobody likes the new playground.
example.answer: Fair: Many students say the new playground has too little shade.

items.prompt: Rewrite each claim so it is fair and strong.
rows: Scientists say our river is the dirtiest ever.
answers: Some people doubt recycling, but it keeps tonnes of waste out of landfill.
Short showers save thousands of litres a year.
Scientists say our river is the dirtiest ever.
Council tests found rubbish and oil in our river.

steps: Write a sneaky ad with three tricks
example.answer: Sneaky: Every kid wants them! Fair: Soft, warm, and they last all winter.

items.prompt: Invent a silly product. Write a sneaky ad with three labelled tricks, then its fair twin.
items.answer: A sneaky ad with three labelled tricks, and a fair version that is still persuasive.

resources.label: Extension
resources.description: Early finisher option: question real-sounding ad claims, then write a fair ad that beats a sneaky one.
resources.title: Ad Investigator
resources.subtitle: Ask the question the advertiser hopes you won't.

example.answer: Which doctors? How many? I'd want a dental association's advice.

items.prompt: For each ad claim, write the question to ask and the proof you'd want.
rows: '9 out of 10 kids prefer Zoom bikes.'
'The most loved cereal in the country.'
answers: '9 out of 10 kids prefer Zoom bikes.'
'The most loved cereal in the country.'
Sales figures or a fair survey

example.prompt: Sneaky: Everyone's switching to Glow Bulbs! Fair: Glow Bulbs use a fifth of the power.
example.answer: The fair one gives a real reason to buy.

items.prompt: Write a fair ad for your Week 3 campaign that is MORE persuasive than a sneaky one. Explain why it works.
items.answer: A fair, vivid ad with a real reason and a call to action, plus a why.

resources.description: Supported option: fair-or-sneaky choices, a first fix done and a frame.
resources.title: Fair or Sneaky Helper
resources.subtitle: Sneaky words: everyone, only, never, experts say.

rows: Only mean people cut down trees.
answers: Only mean people cut down trees.
items.hint: The first one is done for you.

example.answer: Sun Hats keep the sun off your face. Grab one for summer!

items.prompt: Write a fair ad for a product you invent: name it, give one true reason, tell people what to do.
items.hint: Use a true fact about the product.
